accepted_script:
I’m researching AI agents, and the annoying part is that the word “agent” makes everything sound more finished than it is.

An AI that gives you one answer? Useful. But an agent is interesting because it can keep going. It can make decisions, choose tools, search for information, read documents, write information, call APIs, handle multi-step tasks, maintain state, and react when something changes around it.

That is where the experiment starts getting properly weird.

Because the model is only one part of the machine. You might also need memory, search, databases, business rules, user profiles, tools, and regular software holding the whole thing together with what I assume is digital duct tape.

And none of that means it’s right.

A language model can sound extremely confident while misunderstanding the job, losing context, inventing details, or chasing the completely wrong objective. So I’m less interested in asking, “Is this technically an agent?” and more interested in the dangerous question:

What happens when it can actually do something instead of merely talking about doing it?

Then you add more agents. They can share information, divide work, disagree, cooperate, develop strategies—or just create a tiny bureaucratic nightmare at machine speed.

I’m not claiming that proves consciousness. Interesting behavior is already plenty interesting.

So I’m digging through the old workshop-agent notes, figuring out the smallest test that lets one actually make decisions about a project. If you want to see what it does when I give it a little more room to think, stick around.
